title: A novel application of passive acoustic monitoring for detecting tidal constituents through low-frequency ambient noise variability
content:
Abstract
Understanding tidal variability is essential for safe navigation, coastal development, and environmental management. However, traditional tidal observations from tide gauges, pressure sensors, or satellite altimetry remain sparse in many remote polar regions. This study demonstrates that passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) systems, originally developed to record marine mammal vocalizations, can be repurposed as an effective supplementary source of tidal information. We analyzed low-frequency ambient noise (0.5–5 Hz) recorded by long-term PAM moorings in the Scotia and Lazarev Seas to investigate acoustic signatures associated with tidal influences. Noise levels exhibited significant temporal variability, and power spectral analysis revealed distinct cyclic patterns corresponding to major tidal constituents, including the luni-solar diurnal constituent (${{K}_1}$), the principal lunar diurnal constituent (${{O}_1}$), and the solar semidiurnal (${{S}_2}$) and lunar semidiurnal (${{M}_2}$) constituents. These acoustic detections were consistent with co-located conductivity–temperature–depth measurements and predictions from the TPXO tidal model. Our results highlight the potential of low-frequency ambient noise as a proxy for tidal dynamics and demonstrate the practicality, cost-effectiveness, and scientific value of reusing PAM datasets for oceanographic applications. This approach provides a novel and scalable method to augment tidal monitoring in data-sparse regions, particularly in the Southern Ocean.
